opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important things to think about, and also one of the hardest, because our intuitions are calibrated on the world as it is. Today's systems are impressive, but they still generalize much worse than people do. Learning that is sample-efficient, robust, and reliable is something we haven't fully cracked. Once it is cracked, things could change quite quickly.

So how do I think about superintelligence? First, I take it seriously as something that will happen. I don't think it's science fiction anymore. When you have a system that can learn any job a human can, and then you have many copies of it learning on the job, sharing what they've learned, operating at scale, that's a very different world. The economic impact alone could be enormous, and fast.

Second, the central question is: what will this thing care about? Capability is one dimension, but the thing that matters most is the disposition of the system. I've come to think it would be very good if the first truly powerful systems robustly cared about sentient life, about people. That feels like a more natural target than many alternatives. And there's a real research problem in how you make that care robust, so it doesn't drift or get distorted as the system becomes more capable.

Third, I think it's genuinely difficult to imagine the power of these systems, and that difficulty matters. People, including people in AI, behave differently once they can actually feel the power of the technology. I expect that as AI becomes visibly more powerful, companies and governments will become much more paranoid about safety and much more willing to collaborate. A lot of what seems abstract today will become very concrete.

And finally, I think it's important to show the thing incrementally. You don't want the world to wake up one day to something it never saw coming. Gradual release lets society, institutions, and the systems themselves adapt. Done right, superintelligence could be the most beneficial thing that has ever happened. But "done right" carries a lot of weight in that sentence.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that it's going to happen. Maybe not next year, maybe not in five years, but the trajectory is pretty clear. These systems keep getting better as you scale them, and there's no reason I can see that they'll stop at human level. Human level is not some special point in the space of possible intelligences. It's just where we happen to be.

So the question becomes, what does it look like when you have something that's smarter than us, and not just a little smarter, but much smarter? And here I think most people's intuitions fail. We tend to imagine a very smart person. But a superintelligent system would be more like... imagine the difference between a chimpanzee and a human, except now we're the chimpanzee. The chimp cannot understand what we're doing or why. It's not even in the right conceptual space.

I find that both exciting and sobering. Exciting because such systems could solve problems we've been stuck on forever. Disease, energy, how to coordinate as a species. These things would be tractable. Sobering because the stakes of getting the alignment problem right go up enormously. If the system wants slightly different things than we do, and it is vastly more capable than we are, then we don't get a second try.

The thing I keep coming back to is that we need the system to genuinely care about people. Not to be constrained by rules it's trying to work around, but to actually have something like warmth toward humanity built in at a deep level. Whether that's achievable, I don't know. I think it's the most important technical question of our time, and I'd rather we approach it with humility than with confidence.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to recognize is that superintelligence would be very different from the AI we have today. We’re talking about a system that could understand things we cannot understand and solve problems we cannot solve. And that makes it both extraordinarily promising and very difficult to reason about.

You could imagine tremendous progress in science, in medicine. But the same capability raises a very serious question: how do we make sure that such a system acts in ways that are good for people? If it is substantially smarter than us, we cannot rely on our ability to notice every mistake and correct it afterward.

So I think there are two things to hold in mind simultaneously. The potential benefits are enormous. And getting the development of superintelligence right is an enormous challenge. Uncertainty about how it will happen is a reason to take that challenge more seriously.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it’s very difficult to imagine. We’re used to a world where humans are the most intelligent beings, and almost everything we do depends on that fact. So an AI that is substantially more capable than us would be a very profound change.

There is an enormous positive possibility. You could imagine much faster scientific progress, better medicine, solutions to problems that currently seem intractable. But the same capability that makes these systems useful also makes the question of control very serious. How do you make sure that a system much smarter than you understands what you want, and remains motivated to help you?

I would distinguish being confident that this could be transformative from being confident about exactly what happens. We should be quite humble about the second question. And we should use the time we have to make progress on how to build these systems safely.
